Just build vertical farms you nits. You're going to spend twice in fertilizer, which is going to add costs to water run off because now it'll be agri waste and you have to treat it to prevent damage nearby lakes/rivers, than just running a hydroponic/led indoor farm. You can convert those nice outdoor spaces into rain gardens, but you won't be building an effective farm anytime soon.

Vertical farms are appropriate in some situations, and certainly have less runoff than the vacant lot model that people in Detroit are following. They are, however, extremely capital intensive, and a 'moon-shot' idea for most residents of Detroit. Urban farming/gardening is possible for anyone who can afford the price of seed and a shovel, or borrow one in the case of the shovel. It's practical for ordinary people who can't swing a multimillion dollar loan. An "effective farm" has a different meaning for people who are growing for their own consumption or the local market, as opposed to an enterprise producing for a national or international market.

I will grant that vertical farms have less of a runoff problem, but I don't think that twice as much is a reasonable estimate in terms of fertilizer costs. That can be debated of course. I also don't think that the size of whatever acreage might be used in a city like Detroit would significantly increase the cost of sewage treatment. The infrastructure is already in place. This is in contrast to a 'normal' farm where the runoff is simply not treated at all.

Well obviously everybody I think, but first past the post kind of forces this upon us. It's the reason almost no developed nations still use it - it forces strategic voting and requires you vote against your preferred candidate. It's also the reason for a two party system. Imagine there are three candidates. One who really hits your beliefs, one who kind of hits them, and one that's completely opposite of them. Well if about 20% of people are voting for the guy who really hits your belief, 35% for the guy who kind of does and then 45% for the person who's completely opposite of them then you have a simple choice. Vote against your preferred candidate, or get something that's completely opposite of what you want. This also isn't just an abstract scenario. It's pretty common. In this election the number of libertarians leaning individuals that vote for libertarian instead of Trump will likely decide whether the next president is Trump or Clinton. It's a very silly system. I think the only reason we continue to use it is that it perpetuates the power of those who are already in power - the very people that would be required to change our voting system to, for instance, proportional. It's so silly, fewer people than ever identify as republican or democrat yet nearly 100% of seats at all levels of government are filled by them. That's first past the post for you.

I agree with you that FPTP is not a great balloting system, but it doesn't explain why the U.S. has effectively only two parties. You only need to look north, to Canada, to falsify the hypothesis that FPTP leads to a two-party system. I don't know what all the factors are that have led the U.S. to have effectively only two parties (it was not always that way), but FPTP is not the explanation.

Yeah, many FPTP nations have some third party presence but these are inevitably marginalized. In Canada every single government they've had has been either the national liberal or conservative party with one exception during World War 1. Compare FPTP nations to a proportional representation nation like Finland. It's just completely night and day. The peoples' majority views change and thus does their majority representation - something you'll see in just about every single proportional system and in just about no FPTP system. I'm saying "just about" there to cover my bases, but to my knowledge I could change that literally every single FPTP/proportional system.

As an aside, this observation has also been somewhat formalized as Duverger's Law.
